source.title: Asymmetries of the Lower Limb: The Calculation Conundrum in Strength Training and Conditioning

paper.citation: Bishop, C., Read, P., Chavda, S., & Turner, A. (2016). Asymmetries of the lower limb: The calculation conundrum in strength training and conditioning. Strength & Conditioning Journal, 38(6), 27–32. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000264
paper.abstract: Which equations have been used to calculate lower-limb asymmetry, and what interpretive tradeoffs follow? Methodological/practitioner review; no participant sample. Uses a hypothetical 25-cm versus 20-cm jump example. Applies broadly to performance testing but does not validate injury or performance thresholds. Narrative comparison of nine published asymmetry equations. Equations were evaluated conceptually for magnitude, sign, reference value, and longitudinal interpretability. No systematic search or empirical comparison dataset was reported.
paper.tldr: This article explains why asymmetry percentages depend on the equation and reference limb, affecting longitudinal interpretation. The same 25-versus-20-cm scores produced asymmetry outputs from 7.04% to 22.2%, or an 80% symmetry index, depending on equation. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Narrative comparison of nine published asymmetry equations. Equations were evaluated conceptually for magnitude, sign, reference value, and longitudinal interpretability. No systematic search or empirical comparison dataset was reported.
paper.findings: The same 25-versus-20-cm scores produced asymmetry outputs from 7.04% to 22.2%, or an 80% symmetry index, depending on equation. Always placing the stronger/highest limb first removes direction and can conceal a change in favored limb over time. The authors tentatively favored symmetry angle because it avoids a chosen reference value, while acknowledging insufficient evidence to establish one best method.
paper.limitations: Recommendations are conceptual and based on a hypothetical example, not criterion-outcome validation. The article itself states that equation distinctions had not been established and evidence was very limited. Equation choice does not solve task reliability, measurement error, bilateral weakness, or outcome-validity problems. Later testing should preserve the original signed direction and raw limb values, not only a percentage.
paper.practicalImplications: Predefine one equation, keep raw left/right values and sign, and do not compare percentages calculated differently. Interpret change only when it exceeds test-specific error and connects to the decision-relevant task.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Predefine one equation, keep raw left/right values and sign, and do not compare percentages calculated differently. Interpret change only when it exceeds test-specific error and connects to the decision-relevant task. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, predefine one equation, keep raw left/right values and sign, and do not compare percentages calculated differently. Interpret change only when it exceeds test-specific error and connects to the decision-relevant task. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
